patterns.source: project/paper.txt (Level 0 -- the project's own paper; the only source in this run with full read_depth)
patterns.rhetorical_purpose: Report a strong headline number while disclosing, in the same breath, a specific asymmetry that qualifies the comparison.
move_sequence: state the metric and the number (79.3% pass rate)
give the comparison that makes the number meaningful (vs. the best non-agentic baseline, 48.6%)
name the one baseline that scores higher (SWE-Agent, 87.7%)
immediately disclose the specific condition asymmetry that makes that one comparison unequal (1-shot demonstration vs. their own 0-shot)
patterns.reader_question_answered: Is 79.3% good, and is it the best number on this benchmark, and if not, why not?
patterns.assumed_knowledge: pass@k-style benchmark scoring; the concept of few-shot demonstrations
patterns.transition_behavior: uses 'While X achieves Y ... whereas our evaluation ... is 0-shot' as a genuine contrast connective (the contrast is real, not decorative)
patterns.evidence_placement: the qualifying fact sits in the very next sentence after the number it qualifies, not deferred to a separate limitations section
patterns.result_interpretation_pattern: number -> reference point -> the one exception -> why the exception isn't a clean loss
patterns.limitation_framing: the caveat is attached to the specific claim it bounds, in place, rather than stated only as a generic limitation later
patterns.signature: headline number immediately followed by its strongest counter-example and the specific reason the counter-example is not apples-to-apples
patterns.reader_effect: reader trusts the headline number more, because the paper pre-empts the obvious 'but X did better' objection with a concrete reason rather than silence
patterns.repair_principle: when citing a comparator that beats your own result, name the condition difference immediately, not as an afterthought

patterns.rhetorical_purpose: Frame many individual per-benchmark numbers as evidence for one overarching claim, stated before the numbers appear.
move_sequence: state the categories the evaluation spans (software, web, misc.) before any table
state the property under test (one unmodified agent's cross-category performance) before any table
after the tables, explicitly reconnect the numbers to that stated property ('the same CodeAct agent ... demonstrates competitive performance across three major task categories')
name what makes the comparison meaningful (baseline agents are usually built for one category)
patterns.reader_question_answered: Why am I being shown 15 unrelated-looking tables, and what should I conclude from all of them together?
patterns.transition_behavior: the synthesizing sentence after the tables uses 'Notably ... This is particularly significant when compared to' to point back at a contrast set up before the tables were shown
patterns.evidence_placement: the synthesis sentence follows the tables, but the property it synthesizes was already named before the tables, so the reader was reading them prospectively rather than needing a payoff added after the fact
patterns.result_interpretation_pattern: framing sentence (before) -> tables -> synthesis sentence (after) that answers the framing
patterns.figure_table_integration: each mini-table is introduced by one sentence describing the benchmark's task, before its numbers are given
patterns.contribution_framing: the cross-category synthesis functions as the paper's central claim, stated once the reader already has the numbers needed to check it
patterns.signature: state the interpretive frame before the data, then re-state it explicitly after the data, tying the two together with a named contrast
patterns.reader_effect: prevents the 'wall of tables' feeling; the reader always knows which question a given number is supposed to help answer
patterns.repair_principle: never let a run of results-tables stand without a framing sentence before and a synthesis sentence after
